title: What data protection training do Portuguese organizations need under Law 58/2019?
description: What Portugal's GDPR implementation law, Law 58/2019, and CNPD guidance mean for staff training: confidentiality, DPO awareness, workplace data, crimes.
shortAnswer: Portugal's Law 58/2019 implements the GDPR and names the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD) as supervisor. It sets no hours, but it imposes a confidentiality duty on everyone who processes personal data, tasks the data protection officer with raising staff awareness of security incidents, and creates crimes that individual employees can commit. CNPD Guideline 2023/1 expects organizations to build a privacy and security culture and train staff against phishing and email errors.
keyTakeaways: Law 58/2019 of August 8, 2019 ensures the execution of the GDPR in Portugal; the CNPD is the national supervisory authority under Article 3.
Article 10(2) puts every person involved in any processing operation under a duty of confidentiality, which is the core message for all staff.
Article 11(b) makes it a DPO function to sensitize users to the early detection of security incidents and the need to report them immediately.
Articles 46 to 48 create crimes, such as unauthorized access to personal data, punishable by up to one year in prison, doubled for special categories.
CNPD Guideline 2023/1 recommends a staff culture of privacy and security, targeted training after security tests, and email handling training.
regulator: Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD), Portugal's data protection supervisory authority
appliesTo: Controllers and processors established in Portugal, public and private
Employers processing employee data, including payroll and certified accountants acting for them
Public entities, which must designate a data protection officer under Article 12
Health providers and others processing health or genetic data
Every employee, contractor, and officer who takes part in processing personal data

sections.heading: What is Law 58/2019 and how does it relate to the GDPR?

blocks.text: Law 58/2019 (Lei n.º 58/2019, de 8 de agosto) is the Portuguese law that ensures the execution of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), in national law. The GDPR applies directly; Law 58/2019 fills the gaps the Regulation leaves to Member States, such as the supervisory authority, the data protection officer in the public sector, employment data, health data, fines, and crimes. The baseline obligations, including the Article 39 duty of the DPO to train staff, are covered in [GDPR staff training requirements](/regulations/gdpr-staff-training-requirements).

Article 3 of [Law 58/2019](https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2019/08/15100/0000300040.pdf) names the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD) as the national supervisory authority for the GDPR and the law. Article 4 describes it as an independent administrative entity that operates with the Assembly of the Republic and supervises compliance with the GDPR and national data protection rules.

blocks.title: Part of the law is not applied by the CNPD
blocks.text: In Deliberation 2019/494, the CNPD resolved to disapply several provisions of Law 58/2019 that it considers incompatible with the GDPR, including the fine ranges in Articles 37(2) and 38(2), the prior warning rule in Article 39(3), and Article 28(3)(a) on employee consent. As at November 2026, training material should not present those provisions as settled law in proceedings before the CNPD.

sections.heading: What does Law 58/2019 require staff to know?

blocks.text: Law 58/2019 does not prescribe a training course or a number of hours. It does, however, impose duties on individuals that only training can make effective, and it sets national rules that GDPR training written for another country will not cover.

The most important is confidentiality. Article 10(2) states that the DPO, controllers, processors, "e todas as pessoas que intervenham em qualquer operação de tratamento de dados, estão obrigados a um dever de confidencialidade": everyone who takes part in any processing operation is bound by a duty of confidentiality, in addition to any professional secrecy rules. For health and genetic data, Article 29(4) extends a secrecy duty to officers, workers, and service providers of the controller, the DPO, students and researchers, and all health professionals with access to health data.

Staff also need to know the national rules that change how GDPR principles apply in Portugal. Article 16 sets 13 as the age at which a child can consent to information society services. Article 28 limits employee data processing to the purposes and limits in the Labor Code, restricts the use of video surveillance recordings, and allows biometric data of workers only for attendance and access control, using non-reversible representations. Article 29(1) applies a need to know principle to access to health and genetic data.

sections.heading: What role does the data protection officer play in awareness?

blocks.text: The data protection officer (encarregado de proteção de dados) carries a specific awareness function in Portugal. Article 11 adds three functions to those in Articles 37 to 39 of the GDPR: ensuring periodic and unscheduled audits; sensitizing users to the importance of the timely detection of security incidents and the need to inform the security officer immediately; and handling relations with data subjects.

Article 9(1) states that the DPO is designated on the GDPR Article 37(5) criteria and does not need professional certification. Article 12 makes a DPO mandatory in public entities and specifies at least one per ministry, autonomous region department, and municipality, and in parishes where justified, notably those with more than 750 inhabitants. Article 13 repeats the GDPR test for private entities: large scale regular and systematic monitoring, or large scale processing of special category or criminal data.
In practice, the Article 11(b) duty gives the DPO a mandate to run or commission incident awareness training, and it gives an auditor a reason to ask for evidence that it happened.

sections.heading: What does CNPD guidance say about training?

blocks.text: The CNPD's main training guidance is [Guideline 2023/1 on organizational and security measures](https://www.cnpd.pt/umbraco/surface/cnpdDecision/download/122048) (Diretriz/2023/1 sobre medidas organizativas e de segurança aplicáveis aos tratamentos de dados pessoais), approved on January 10, 2023. It explains that the main attack vectors it saw in 2022 included the lack of user training to detect phishing campaigns, and it recommends measures to meet the security duties in Article 32 of the GDPR.

items: Organizational measure (i): run systematic IT security audits and penetration tests, so that the organization can invest in training with specific content targeted at the vulnerabilities found.
Organizational measure (m): foster a culture of privacy and information security among staff, so each person can recognize potential threats and act on them, reducing human error.
Organizational measure (n): make workers aware of the confidentiality duty that applies because they process personal data.
Email measure (f): train workers to operate email sending mechanisms according to defined procedures, alert them to the most common errors that cause data breaches, and encourage double checking.

blocks.text: The Guideline is a recommendation, not a binding rule, and it states that its list is neither exhaustive nor static. It is still the clearest statement of what the Portuguese supervisor expects to see when it assesses whether security measures were appropriate after a breach.

sections.heading: What are the penalties, and why do they matter for individual staff?

blocks.text: Organizations face GDPR administrative fines, and individuals face criminal liability under Portuguese law. That second point is what makes Law 58/2019 training different from generic GDPR awareness.

Law 58/2019 classifies offenses as very serious (Article 37) and serious (Article 38). Breaching the GDPR Article 32 security rules, failing breach notification duties under Article 33, and failing the DPO duties in Articles 37 to 39 are serious offenses under Article 38(1). The law's own fine ranges in Articles 37(2) and 38(2) are among the provisions the CNPD disapplies in [Deliberation 2019/494](https://www.cnpd.pt/umbraco/surface/cnpdDecision/download/121704), so the CNPD applies the GDPR Article 83 maximums directly. Article 44(1) states that fines apply equally to public and private entities.

The crimes are aimed at people. Article 46 punishes using personal data in a way incompatible with the purpose of collection; Article 47 punishes accessing personal data without due authorization or justification; Article 48 punishes copying, removing, ceding, or transferring personal data without legal basis or consent. Each carries up to one year in prison or a fine of up to 120 days, doubled where special category or criminal data is involved. Staff who browse records out of curiosity or forward customer lists to a personal account need to hear this plainly.

sections.heading: How should a Portuguese organization build its data protection training?

blocks.text: Start from the GDPR baseline, then add a Portuguese layer that covers the points above. A practical sequence follows.

items: Record each Law 58/2019 and CNPD source in the [compliance obligations register](/glossary/compliance-obligations-register) with the article number.
Give every new joiner a short module on the Article 10(2) confidentiality duty and the Article 46 to 48 crimes, and record acknowledgment.
Have the DPO own an incident awareness plan under Article 11(b), with a single reporting route that staff can name.
Add role modules for HR (Article 28), health data handlers (Article 29), and staff who send personal data by email (Guideline 2023/1).
Use phishing test results to target follow up training, as Guideline 2023/1 measure (i) describes, and keep the before and after data.
Set refresh intervals in the training policy using [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

blocks.text: Portuguese employers can count data protection training toward the Labor Code's annual training entitlement where it meets that regime's conditions; see [Portugal's Labor Code continuous training](/regulations/portugal-labour-code-continuous-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each Law 58/2019 article and CNPD recommendation to a defined concept, learning outcome, and assessment point before any content is written, so the Portuguese layer is visible next to the GDPR baseline. Each item carries its source and review date, which makes it easier to show the CNPD what staff were taught and when.

faqs.q: Does Law 58/2019 require a set number of training hours?
faqs.a: No. Neither Law 58/2019 nor the GDPR sets hours. The duty is to make confidentiality, security, and DPO functions effective, which in practice means documented training sized to risk. CNPD Guideline 2023/1 points to regular culture building and targeted training after security tests.

faqs.q: Does a Portuguese DPO need a certification?
faqs.a: No. Article 9(1) of Law 58/2019 states that the DPO is designated on the GDPR Article 37(5) criteria, professional qualities and expert knowledge, without needing professional certification. The DPO acts with technical autonomy whatever the contractual relationship.

faqs.q: Can an employee be prosecuted for misusing personal data in Portugal?
faqs.a: Yes. Articles 46 to 48 of Law 58/2019 make it a crime to use data for incompatible purposes, to access data without authorization or justification, or to copy or transfer data without legal basis. Penalties reach one year in prison, doubled for special category data.

faqs.q: Why does the CNPD not apply some articles of Law 58/2019?
faqs.a: In Deliberation 2019/494 the CNPD concluded that certain provisions conflict with the GDPR, which takes precedence, and resolved not to apply them in cases it assesses. The list includes the national fine ranges, the prior warning rule, and the employee consent rule in Article 28(3)(a).
